title: Tesla Unveils Flying Roadster with SpaceX Thrusters After Years of Delays
author: The Quest for Profit
excerpt: Tesla has unveiled its redesigned Roadster with SpaceX-inspired thrusters and hovering capabilities. Elon Musk says production is planned for 2028.

content.text: Tesla has unveiled a redesigned version of its long-delayed Roadster, presenting a high-performance electric sports car equipped with thrusters and technology intended to let it lift off the ground. Chief Executive Elon Musk introduced the vehicle at a demonstration at a SpaceX test facility in Texas on October 15, showcasing aerial maneuvers that included lifting, rotating and landing using compressed air propulsion technology. The unveiling attracted attention because Musk has repeatedly suggested that the next-generation Roadster would push beyond the conventional limits of automotive engineering.

The demonstration featured a two-seat sports car climbing a steep ramp, remaining inverted briefly and using thrusters to return to the ground. Tesla also showed the vehicle jumping over a line of other company models. The demonstrations were conducted without a human driver inside the car, with Musk explaining that the precautions were intended to prevent injuries if the maneuvers failed.

Despite the spectacle, important questions remain about the Roadster's practical flying capabilities, regulatory status and eventual commercial availability. Tesla says production is planned for 2028, nearly nine years after the company first introduced the next-generation vehicle in 2017. The latest unveiling represents a significant milestone for the project, but the company has yet to establish that its most ambitious aerial features will be suitable for ordinary road use or sustained flight.
SpaceX Thrusters and Suction Technology Power the Roadster Demonstration

The redesigned Roadster combines electric-car engineering with technology developed through Tesla's collaboration with SpaceX. According to CNN Business and Axios, the vehicle uses high-pressure compressed air released through thrusters to produce thrust, while an underbody suction system helps hold the car against surfaces during extreme maneuvers. The combination was demonstrated during the Texas unveiling, where the vehicle climbed a steep ramp, hung upside down briefly and rotated before returning to the ground.

Musk said the Roadster could accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in approximately 0.8 seconds, placing it among the most ambitious performance vehicles Tesla has announced. The company also claims a top speed exceeding 230 mph. These are manufacturer's claims, and their real-world performance will need to be assessed when production-ready vehicles become available.

The technology is intended to distinguish the Roadster from conventional electric sports cars. Rather than relying exclusively on wheel traction and traditional aerodynamic systems, the proposed design incorporates propulsion technology to improve acceleration and enable brief aerial movements. The suction system is intended to increase grip during demanding driving maneuvers.

However, a demonstration of lifting or briefly leaving the ground is not equivalent to sustained flight. CNN noted that the vehicle has not demonstrated long-range airborne travel, while Axios reported that the flying version is not approved for public roads. The engineering challenge will be translating a dramatic demonstration into a practical, reliable, and legally compliant vehicle.
Nearly Nine Years of Delays Put Tesla's Roadster Back in the Spotlight

Tesla first unveiled the next-generation Roadster in November 2017, promising a high-performance electric vehicle with exceptional speed and range. The company initially indicated that deliveries would begin in 2020, but the project repeatedly slipped as Tesla concentrated on other vehicles and production priorities. Musk subsequently discussed additional technologies, including SpaceX-inspired thrusters, which added further complexity to an already ambitious program.

The prolonged development period has made the Roadster one of Tesla's most closely watched unfinished projects. Customers were allowed to place reservations for years before production, with deposits reported at $50,000 for standard reservations and substantially more for certain limited editions. The latest unveiling has renewed interest in the vehicle, but it also leaves questions about delivery schedules, final pricing, and the availability of the most advanced features.

Tesla says production is planned for 2028. That target remains prospective rather than a confirmed delivery date, particularly given the program's history of delays. The company has not provided a complete set of final specifications covering every version, and the eventual production configuration could differ from the vehicle shown during the demonstration.

The Roadster also has symbolic importance for Tesla. Its original model helped establish the company as a manufacturer of performance electric vehicles, and the redesigned version is intended to showcase its engineering capabilities. However, Musk has acknowledged that the car is unlikely to transform Tesla's finances on its own. Its significance may therefore lie as much in demonstrating technological ambition as in generating sales revenue.
Safety, Regulatory Approval and Commercial Viability Remain Uncertain

Although the Roadster demonstration attracted attention, its proposed flying capabilities raise substantial questions about safety and regulation. A vehicle that leaves the ground must address challenges that conventional cars do not face, including stability during flight, controlled landing, occupant protection, and the consequences of propulsion-system failure. The requirements become more complicated when a vehicle is designed to operate both on public roads and in the air.

CNN reported that aviation specialists remain skeptical about whether a road-legal sports car could provide meaningful sustained flight. Cars require structural features such as bumpers and crumple zones, while aircraft must minimize weight and maintain aerodynamic efficiency. Combining these requirements creates engineering compromises that could limit performance in both environments.

Regulatory approval is another obstacle. Axios reported that Tesla's proposed Rocket version, which includes the flying system, is not approved for public roads. Tesla has described different versions of the Roadster, including configurations intended for road use and a more experimental model with the ability to lift off the ground. Their eventual availability will depend on the final specifications, safety requirements, and applicable regulations.

Cost and practicality will also influence demand. Tesla has not disclosed a final price for the redesigned vehicle, and the specialized propulsion system could make the most advanced version expensive and difficult to maintain. Until the company demonstrates reliable performance outside a controlled event and provides firm production details, the Roadster should be viewed as an ambitious technology project rather than an established flying-car solution.

For Tesla, the next milestones will be demonstrating the technology's reliability, clarifying regulatory requirements, and meeting the proposed 2028 production target. The unveiling has renewed interest in the Roadster, but its commercial success will depend on whether the company can turn the spectacle into a safe, practical and deliverable product.
